claims.text: Successful formation of noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles requires synchronized reduction kinetics among all metal precursors.
A transient amorphous or sub-stoichiometric intermediate can synchronize precursor reduction.
The transient intermediate locks the components into a uniformly mixed nucleation event before elemental segregation occurs.
Changing a process parameter can alter both overall reduction kinetics and stabilization of the transient intermediate.
Modulating reduction kinetics promotes simultaneous nucleation of all metal species.
The transient intermediate prevents premature or nonuniform reduction.
Preventing premature or nonuniform reduction reduces phase separation and elemental segregation.
Phase separation and elemental segregation are a common cause of heterogeneous outcomes in multimetal systems.
The modified treatment will produce a more homogeneous elemental distribution than the unchanged baseline.
The modified treatment will reduce phase separation relative to the unchanged baseline.
Greater compositional homogeneity and reduced phase separation indicate successful formation of a high-entropy alloy structure.
A standard thermal-treatment baseline typically produces some phase segregation, elemental clustering, or uncontrolled morphology.
The proposed mechanism applies when precursor reduction rates and intermediate formation dominate alloy homogeneity in noble-metal systems.
The proposed mechanism is not expected to apply when solvent–ligand interactions or alternative reaction pathways override kinetic control.
Exceptionally fast or instantaneous reduction can place a system outside the proposed mechanism's domain.
The required intermediate-stabilization timescale and energetic thresholds for synchronization have not been quantified.
Precursor chemistry and substrate effects may alter the outcome.
